## Example 5.1: Building enthalpies from a reference state

Air is heated in a steady-state duct heater from 25 $^\circ$C to 150 $^\circ$C at a
mass flow rate of 0.50 kg s$^{-1}$. $C_P = 1.01$ kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

Using a reference state of **air, gas, 0 $^\circ$C, 1 atm**:


1. Tabulate the absolute enthalpy of the inlet and outlet streams.
2. Calculate the required heat, $\dot{Q}$.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

**System and assumptions**

The system is the duct heater. Steady state, one stream in and one out, no work
($\dot{W}=0$), no phase change, no reaction. The general balance

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{Q} + \dot{W}$$

collapses to

$$0 = \dot{m}H_{in} - \dot{m}H_{out} + \dot{Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\dot{Q} = \dot{m}\left(H_{out} - H_{in}\right)$$

**Part 1 — enthalpy relative to the reference state**

With $H_{ref} \equiv 0$ at $T_{ref} = 0\ ^\circ$C, each stream enthalpy is the sensible
heat needed to bring air from the reference temperature to its actual temperature:

$$H = \int_{T_{ref}}^{T} C_P\,dT = C_P\left(T - T_{ref}\right)$$

| Stream | $T$ ($^\circ$C) | $H = C_P(T - T_{ref})$ (kJ kg$^{-1}$) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Inlet  | 25  | $1.01(25 - 0) = 25.3$ |
| Outlet | 150 | $1.01(150 - 0) = 151.5$ |

These are *not* absolute enthalpies of air in any physical sense — they are enthalpies
measured from the zero we chose.

**Part 2 — heat requirement**

$$\dot{Q} = \dot{m}\left(H_{out} - H_{in}\right) = 0.50\left(151.5 - 25.3\right)$$

$$\dot{Q} = 63.1\ \text{kW}$$

**Check**

The sign is positive, meaning heat is transferred *into* the system — correct for a
heater. The magnitude is plausible: a domestic fan heater is a few kW, an industrial
duct heater tens of kW.

Note also that $151.5 - 25.3 = 126.2$ kJ kg$^{-1}$, which is exactly
$C_P(T_{out} - T_{in}) = 1.01 \times 125$. The reference state cancelled — as it must.

:::
:::
